quote: Wie variirt der Kreis, wenn man einen Parameter $t$ in die Coefficienten einführt und denselben variirt?
english: How does the circle vary if one introduces a parameter t into the coefficients and varies it?
topic: A list of research and dissertation topics: the discriminant and invariants of the quartic, Poincaré cycles of differential equations, rotation of a body filled with fluid, three number-theoretic doctoral topics (class fields, Fermat's theorem, Weber's theorem), and independence of the laws 1-17 for complex number systems.

triage.modern_statement: This is read from context, since the page sits next to 'Poincaré cycles of differential equations'. Take a planar polynomial (or analytic) system dx/dt = P(x,y), dy/dt = Q(x,y), and assume 'Kreis' means a closed cycle, especially a limit cycle in Poincaré's sense. Now let the coefficients depend on a real parameter t. How does the cycle change as t varies? In particular: does it persist and deform smoothly, change its stability, merge with another cycle and vanish, shrink into a focus, or grow into a separatrix loop? And how do limit cycles appear and disappear? In modern terms this is the dependence of limit cycles on parameters, i.e. the bifurcation theory of limit cycles in planar vector fields.
triage.answered_by: There is no single solution. The question became a whole field, bifurcation theory of limit cycles. Poincaré himself studied what is now called the Hopf bifurcation in the late 19th century. Andronov and coworkers proved the bifurcation theorem in two dimensions, and E. Hopf (1942) extended it to any dimension. Andronov and Leontovich wrote on how limit cycles depend on parameters ('Some cases of the dependence of the limit cycles upon parameters', Uchenye Zapiski Gor'kovskogo Universiteta 6, 1937, pp. 3–24). Their school then developed the general 'Theory of Bifurcations of Dynamical Systems on the Plane' (Andronov, Leontovich, Gordon, Maier). Pontryagin gave a criterion for limit cycles that arise when Hamiltonian systems are perturbed (1934). Together these cover the three basic ways limit cycles bifurcate: from a focus (Andronov–Hopf), from a separatrix loop, and from a multiple cycle (saddle-node of cycles). The question is closely tied to the second part of Hilbert's 16th problem (1900), but it is not the same as that problem.

evidence.claim: Poincaré introduced limit cycles in the late 1800s, and the analysis of limit-cycle bifurcation has been a long-standing, challenging problem ever since.
Poincaré studied Hopf bifurcations in the late 19th century. Andronov and coworkers proved the Hopf bifurcation theorem for planar ODE systems, and Hopf extended it to arbitrary dimension.
Hopf bifurcation, also called Poincaré–Andronov–Hopf bifurcation: a stable fixed point loses stability as a parameter varies, and a limit cycle is born at the same time.

A. A. Andronov and E. A. Leontovich, 'Some cases of the dependence of the limit cycles upon parameters', Uchenye Zapiski Gor'kovskogo Universiteta 6 (1937), 3–24. Also cited: Andronov, Leontovich, Gordon, Maier, Theory of Bifurcations of Dynamical Systems on the Plane.
Andronov and Leontovich, 'Dependence of limit cycles on a parameter', is cited as a basic reference on bifurcations of ODE systems.
Limit cycles bifurcate in three ways: Andronov–Hopf bifurcation, bifurcation from a homoclinic or heteroclinic orbit, and bifurcation of a multiple limit cycle.
Bifurcation theory, including the Pontryagin criterion, is closely tied to the second part of Hilbert's 16th problem, one of the most persistent problems on Hilbert's list.

triage.why: Reading 'Kreis' as a Poincaré limit cycle comes from the neighbouring item on Poincaré cycles; this interpretation is mine, not taken from a source. Under that reading, the note asks a general question, how a cycle depends on a parameter in the coefficients, rather than a sharply posed problem. The sources show that Poincaré, Andronov and Leontovich (1937), Pontryagin (1934), Hopf (1942) and the Andronov school answered it systematically by building bifurcation theory, so in that sense it is settled. It is not literally one of Hilbert's 23 problems, but it is closely linked to the second part of the 16th problem (how many limit cycles a polynomial system can have and where they lie). That problem is still open, and research on bifurcations of limit cycles remains very active. Confidence is medium rather than high because the note is short and the identification rests on context.
